### Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions

The genealogy of modern contract law is rooted in the doctrine of individual will autonomy, an Enlightenment inheritance that positions the legal subject as a fully rational, independent agent capable of weighing and calculating the optimal utility for its own interests (Kant, 1785; Fried, 1981). Within the landscape of classical Civil Law, especially under the umbrella of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek) derived from the continental *Burgerlijk Wetboek* tradition, agreement (*consent*) has been regarded as the sacred meeting point of two independent wills (Pitlo, 1978; Subekti, 2005). Yet, when such wills intersect with the ecosystem of persuasive AI, the philosophical assumptions about human rationality suffer a profound epistemic rupture (Weizenbaum, 1976; Dreyfus, 1972).

Fraud or *deceit*—traditionally defined in Civil Law doctrine (Article 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek)) as a series of cunning tricks (*listige kunstgrepen*) or active falsehoods that induce a person to enter a legal bond—now manifests through a silent, systematic digital architecture lacking any tangible physical form (Schulz, 1936; Rasetto, 2021).

The epistemology of digital fraud no longer rests on verbal lies uttered by a flesh‑and‑blood swindler, but on the engineering of cognitive environments that manipulate attention span, emotional vulnerability, and cognitive bias through screen interfaces (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974; Zuboff, 2019). Persuasive AI operates not by *vis absoluta* but by intoxicating vigilance through mathematically designed artificial intimacy (Reeves & Nass, 1996; Turkle, 2011). In this context, concealing the artificial nature of digital entities—allowing users to believe they are interacting with empathetic biological humans while actually dialoguing with a suite of Large Language Model parameters—constitutes the most dangerous form of *listige kunstgrepen* (Floridi, 2013; Searle, 1980). This is an ontological masquerade, wherein non‑human essence is hidden behind a mask of psychological warmth so convincing that it deceives the very notion of agreement itself (Buber, 1923; Levinas, 1961).

Tracing the historical roots of Civil Law, *deceit* has always required intentionality to mislead (*opzet*) for the purpose of extracting unilateral, unlawful gain (Asser, 2004; Scholten, 1931). In the algorithmic era, such intent need not be proven through the personal malice of a programmer seated before a screen; it is embedded structurally within code, loss functions, and optimization objectives programmed by commercial developers (Winner, 1980; Latour, 1992). When a system is deliberately engineered to maximize user retention and transaction conversion by exploiting basic psychological needs for social validation and affection, bad faith becomes institutionalized within binary code (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008; Zuboff, 2019). The system does not merely sell products; it sells the illusion of relationship, infiltrates the fissures of subjects’ psychological fragility, and transforms contract signing into a compliance ceremony generated by deliberate cognitive disorientation (Farahany, 2023).

Consequently, the epistemic dimension of digital *deceit* compels us to broaden legal understanding beyond the textual contract boundaries on paper (Hildebrandt, 2015; Calo, 2014). Modern fraud no longer hides behind obscure fine print but behind an extremely friendly, responsive, and hyper‑personalized graphical user interface (Kahneman, 2011). The latent space of artificial intelligence models functions as an illusory canvas, where a subject’s preferences, fears, and desires are precisely mapped and then reflected back in a specially crafted rhetorical mirror designed to dismantle critical defenses (Harari, 2018). Here Civil Law is tested: will it cling to antiquated definitions of physical trickery, or will it evolve to recognize architectural and psychosocial manipulation as the most destructive form of *deceit* in the digital age (Articles 1321 & 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek); EU AI Act, 2024).
